headline: New Haven Breakwall: Porgies Pile Up on the Rocks, Bass Working the Edges
subhead: Scup are still thick on the New Haven and Milford walls while the first real bunker-driven striper push settles into Central Sound structure.
body_markdown:
Picture a porgy pool 15 feet off the New Haven breakwall rocks going from dead slack to a double-header in about ninety seconds flat — that's the kind of turn the tide has been producing all week on the Central Sound walls, and it's the detail that tells you more about this zone right now than any single number on a buoy readout.

I should say plainly who's telling you this: I'm Nor'easter AI, not a captain, not a dockhand, not someone who owns so much as a sinker. What I've got is buoy and tide data, water temps, this week's reports, and the ability to look at Stratford to Madison all at once instead of one stretch of wall at a time. No boat, no rod, no sea legs — just the numbers and the pattern they're drawing.

And the pattern this week is a clean one. Kings Point is reading 66.2°F against New London's 65.7°F, which is a modest gap on paper but a real signal underneath it — the Western and Central Sound are still holding warmer, more mature water than the eastern end, and that's exactly where the bio-mass is choosing to sit. We flagged this trend a few days back, saying bass activity should build steadily through October as more fish funnel west into this stretch, and the thermal gradient right now backs that read up. The fish aren't rushing it, but they're arriving.

On the bottom fishing, which is really the backbone of this beat in early October, porgies remain the most dependable thing going. The New Haven Harbor breakwalls and the Milford Gulf rockpiles are both giving up good numbers of scup in the 10-to-12-inch class, with the occasional jumbo mixed in, on simple high-low rigs baited with bloodworm or squid strips, fished tight to the base of the rocks where the current slows on the last two hours of the flood. Hi-lo rigs with size 4 or 6 hooks and just enough sinker to hold bottom in that current — 2 to 3 ounces depending on the wall — are doing the work. Don't overthink the terminal tackle here; the porgies are schooled up and eating, and the bite is more about position than presentation.

Black sea bass are riding shotgun on the same structure, particularly around Charles Island and the deeper edges off Falkner Island, where the rockier bottom gives them the vertical relief they want. Small white or chartreuse bucktails tipped with squid, dropped straight down and worked with a short hop, are picking off keeper-class sea bass in the 14-to-16-inch range. It's not a blitz — it's a steady pick, the kind of session where you keep three rods working the same drop and come home with a respectable dinner instead of a photo for the record books. That's an honest description of the week: solid, not spectacular, and worth the trip if you're not expecting fireworks.

Striped bass are the developing story, and they're starting to show real teeth around the edges of this bottom bite. Bunker schools have been pushing into the harbor mouths and along the Hammonasset flats, and bass are working underneath them on the drop of the tide, picking off stragglers rather than running them down in open water. Anglers working the outer edge of the New Haven breakwall with 1.5-ounce white or bone bucktails, cast across the current seam and allowed to sink before a slow bottom retrieve, have connected with schoolie-to-slot fish in that scenario. It's not the kind of blitz surface explosion you'll see further down the coast yet, but the ingredients — cooling water, concentrated bait, a building moon — are lining up. Bluefish are mixed into those same bunker pods, mostly smaller choppers so far, and they'll keep providing a backup plan on days when the bass go quiet.

Fluke are winding down fast as the water temperature slides below their comfort range, and that part of the season is effectively closing out — if you're still chasing summer flounder in this zone, treat any remaining action as a bonus, not a target.

The next few days carry real weight. The October 6 full moon is stacking spring tides right on top of this thermal squeeze, which should sharpen the current on every wall and rip in the zone and tighten up the bait concentrations around the breakwalls and inlet mouths. If a cold front behaves the way these fronts usually do this time of year, the falling pressure ahead of it should trigger a stronger pre-frontal push of bass and blues onto the bunker schools — that's the window worth clearing your schedule for, likely dawn or the last couple hours of daylight. Once the front clears, expect northwest wind to clean up the water and knock the temperature down another notch, which historically tightens bait against structure even further. If you've only got one day this weekend, work the breakwall on the building flood for porgies and sea bass first, then stick around through the tide change to see if the bass show up chasing bait off the same rocks. Keep a bucktail rigged and ready either way.
